findings.title: Every authenticated merchant request performs a PostgreSQL row lock plus an unconditional row UPDATE — a write per read on one table
findings.current_state: validate_and_rotate_merchant_session does SELECT * FROM public.sessions WHERE token = p_token FOR UPDATE (175_fix_session_rpc_search_path.sql:58-62) and then, on every accepted call, UPDATE public.sessions SET token=..., last_active=v_now, ... (:119-124) — the UPDATE is outside the rotation IF and runs unconditionally. The gateway calls this on every request carrying X-LetBuyy-Internal-Session-Token (middleware/auth.ts:136) and follows it with a second query against users_custom (:138-142). Both go through getSupabaseAdmin — PostgREST over HTTP, not a pooled connection.
findings.expected_state: A session-validation path across the 100 -> 10,000 merchant envelope should be a cached or index-only read, not a write plus an exclusive row lock.
findings.risk: Merchant-path throughput is bounded by PostgreSQL write capacity on one table rather than by read capacity. Every dashboard page fanning out N parallel API calls takes N exclusive locks on the SAME session row, serializing them and adding lock-wait latency that grows with UI fan-out. The write amplification also drives WAL volume, autovacuum load and index bloat on sessions proportional to total authenticated request volume.
findings.recommendation: Split the hot path: make validation a read-only function with no FOR UPDATE and no UPDATE, and move last_active maintenance to a coarse update (only when the stored value is older than ~60s) or to an async touch. Consider caching accepted (token -> userId, email, exp) in the CACHE KV namespace for a short TTL.
findings.trigger: Merchant dashboard concurrency above a stated threshold, or measured lock wait on public.sessions.
findings.verification: Falsify by finding a read-only validation path. Confirm with pg_locks sampling during a dashboard load.

findings.title: Telemetry writes 1-2 PostgreSQL rows on every API request, so database write load scales with total request volume rather than commerce volume
findings.current_state: The observability middleware is mounted globally at services/api-gateway/src/index.ts:655 and always inserts one runtime_telemetry_metrics row (middleware/observability.ts:265-302 -> execution/observability-execution.adapter.ts:125-143), plus one worker_request_logs row for everything except anonymous storefront GET/HEAD, which is sampled at 2% (observability.ts:338-381, :199-204; wrangler.toml:61). Migration 131's AFTER-ROW mirror trigger doubles each write with a retention_policies SELECT plus a shadow INSERT carrying an FK check to sites and 3-index maintenance (079:489-503); both policies are registered (079:517-524, 080:48-50) so the early return does not apply. Queue batches add two more inserts each (queue-workers/src/index.ts:292-315). Net cost is roughly 6 statements for a typical recorded request and 3 for a sampled-out anonymous storefront read — for data Analytics Engine already receives at zero database cost (observability.ts:254-263; RUNTIME_TELEMETRY bound at wrangler.toml:212,341).
findings.expected_state: Telemetry should not compete with commerce transactions for the one PostgreSQL. The Analytics Engine dataset is already declared in production configuration.
assumptions: The pool-saturation mechanism in the original claim is REFUTED: these inserts use supabase-js/PostgREST over HTTP (lib/supabase.ts:13-19 -> supabase-adapter/index.ts:34), NOT the postgres client whose pool is capped at max=5 (pooled-sql-adapter/index.ts:41,52, used only by tenant-transaction.ts and storefront.ts). Contention is at shared PostgreSQL write capacity, not that pool.
The writes run in waitUntil after the response (:268, :304, :349), so they add no in-band latency to the generating request; impact is indirect via shared database capacity.

'Dominant PostgreSQL load' is INFERRED, not verified: authenticated requests also perform session/users_custom/rbac/store-context reads plus an audit_logs insert per request, and no load measurement exists in the repository.
Whether current-month shadow partitions exist is UNKNOWN; if they do not, the doubled write buys nothing (ARCH-RESEARCH-035).
findings.risk: PostgreSQL write load scales with total request volume, not with commerce volume. 07_CAPACITY_MODEL.md §3.5 computes that at Band A (~1,787 origin RPS) telemetry alone would consume the entire write budget of a Large-tier instance before a single order is placed. It also compounds ARCH-RESEARCH-012 (no retention) and ARCH-RESEARCH-013 (mirror doubling).
findings.recommendation: Route telemetry to the already-declared, already-bound RUNTIME_TELEMETRY Analytics Engine dataset and stop the per-request PostgreSQL insert, or at minimum apply the existing REQUEST_LOG_SAMPLE_RATE mechanism to runtime_telemetry_metrics, which is currently unsampled. This is the cheapest major capacity fix in the packet. Disable the mirror triggers on the two telemetry tables at the same time.
findings.trigger: Origin request rate above a stated threshold, or PostgreSQL write utilisation above 50% (measurable only after ARCH-RESEARCH-015).
findings.verification: Falsify by exhibiting sampling on runtime_telemetry_metrics. Confirm by counting inserts per request against a staging deploy.

findings.title: Latency degradation converts directly into pooler connection exhaustion, and transaction-mode pooling forbids the session-level primitives an inventory design would reach for
findings.current_state: Primary-source vendor properties accessed 2026-08-16: Supabase direct connections move 60 -> 500 across the entire compute ladder and plateau at 500 from 12XL upward; Supavisor pooler client slots move 200 -> 12,000; the Large tier (~$111/month) has 2 dedicated cores, 160 max_connections and roughly 64 usable pooled server connections after PostgREST/Auth/Storage/Realtime. Transaction-mode pooling never supports session-level advisory locks, PREPARE/DEALLOCATE, LISTEN or temp tables, and Supavisor does not support prepared statements. Cloudflare Hyperdrive independently does not support advisory locks or LISTEN/NOTIFY. Disk autoscale triggers at 90% utilisation with a maximum of 4 modifications per rolling 24 hours; at disk-full the project enters read-only mode and clears only below 95%.
findings.expected_state: Capacity planning must treat the vertical ladder as cores, RAM and IOPS — not as concurrency — and any hot-SKU contention design must avoid session-level advisory locks.
evidence: evidence/21-vendor-digest.md (Supabase compute ladder, Supavisor limits, transaction-mode restrictions; Cloudflare Hyperdrive restrictions)
assumptions: Vendor figures are primary-source as of 2026-08-16 and are not measured against this account.
Which Supabase compute tier is provisioned is UNKNOWN from the repository.
findings.risk: A single slow RPC that pushes mean connection hold time from 20 ms to 400 ms consumes the entire Large-tier pooler allowance at the same request rate — the classic cascade of one slow query to pool exhaustion to every tenant's checkout failing. Beyond ~500 direct connections the only levers are pooling discipline, shorter transactions, and read replicas, which the Constitution currently forbids. Any inventory or checkout design that reaches for a session-level advisory lock will fail on both poolers; hot-SKU contention must be solved with row locks, optimistic version columns or sharded counters.
findings.recommendation: Record these as hard design constraints in 12_TRIGGER_BASED_EVOLUTION.md before any inventory or checkout redesign. Shorten the order transaction (ARCH-RESEARCH-071, -072) as the primary lever, since hold time and not request rate is what exhausts the pooler. Note the live tension recorded in C-6: Cloudflare recommends the Direct connection string, Supabase's scaling story is Supavisor, and the current data layer uses neither — it uses PostgREST, which cannot issue SET LOCAL ROLE and is very likely the real reason app_tenant has no callers (ARCH-RESEARCH-001).
findings.trigger: Mean connection hold time above 100 ms, or pooler client-slot utilisation above 60%.
findings.verification: Falsify against current vendor documentation. Confirm by measuring hold time and slot utilisation once ARCH-RESEARCH-015 is instrumented.

findings.title: Hyperdrive's query cache does not invalidate on write, so a single cached binding for read-after-write paths would be a money bug
findings.current_state: Primary-source vendor properties accessed 2026-08-16: Hyperdrive maintains ~100 origin connections per configuration on the Workers Paid plan, independent of Worker isolate count, at no extra cost. Its query cache defaults to max_age 60 s with stale_while_revalidate 15 s and supports max_age up to 3,600 s. Cloudflare documents explicitly that Hyperdrive 'does not purge or invalidate cached read query results when your application writes to your database'. services/api-gateway/wrangler.toml binds a single HYPERDRIVE configuration for production (:322-324).
findings.expected_state: Any read that must reflect a write — cart, inventory, order status, auth — requires a second --caching-disabled Hyperdrive binding, distinct from the cached binding used for catalog reads.
evidence: evidence/21-vendor-digest.md (Cloudflare Hyperdrive: ~100 origin connections; no write invalidation)
assumptions: Whether the bound configuration has caching enabled or disabled is not determinable from wrangler.toml — it is a Hyperdrive-side setting. That is UNKNOWN and is precisely why this needs an explicit decision rather than an assumption.
Today only four storefront read paths use the pooled SQL adapter (routes/storefront.ts:646,656,671,691), so the current blast radius is small; the risk is on adoption.
findings.risk: Hyperdrive's ~100 origin connections is the single most favourable number in the stack and is the reason the Workers tier is not a bottleneck. But if the cached binding is ever used for a read-after-write path, a shopper can see a stale cart, stale inventory or a stale order status for up to the configured max_age, and an inventory read could authorise an oversell.
findings.recommendation: Declare two Hyperdrive bindings explicitly — one cached for catalog and content reads, one --caching-disabled for cart, inventory, order status and auth — and record which paths may use which. Do this before widening pooled-SQL adoption for ARCH-RESEARCH-001.
findings.trigger: Before any read-after-write path is moved onto pooled SQL.
findings.verification: Falsify against current Hyperdrive documentation. Confirm by reading the Hyperdrive configuration's caching setting in the Cloudflare account.

findings.title: Wave-5 dual-schema losers all survive: the orders.store_id sync trigger, users_custom, payment_transactions and sessions_v2

findings.title: R2 object keys are user-scoped, not site-scoped, and MIME validation trusts the client-declared content type
findings.current_state: Upload keys are ${folder}/${auth.user.id}/${Date.now()}-${uuid}.${ext} (services/api-gateway/src/routes/upload.ts:168), with store_id recorded only in customMetadata (:196-203). Shipping labels use a flat shipping-labels/${labelId}.pdf (routes/shipping-labels.ts:224); retrieval fetches the row by id and only then calls resolveTenantContextForOwnedSite (:379-384), so tenancy is enforced by the application check, not by the key space. validateUploadMime(file) inspects only file.type — the client-supplied multipart Content-Type (lib/upload-mime.ts:70-88) — with no magic-byte sniff, so the SVG hard-block is bypassable by lying about Content-Type. Media objects are served publicly from ASSET_PUBLIC_BASE_URL (cdn.letbuyy.com), relying on a 122-bit UUID for unguessability. No R2 lifecycle or expiry configuration exists in the repository.
findings.expected_state: For a multi-tenant platform with DPDP erasure obligations, object keys should carry site_id so a tenant's blobs can be enumerated and erased by prefix; content type should be validated from the bytes.
assumptions: R2 holds derived artifacts (labels, exports, media), not business truth, so this is not a second data authority.
DELETE does perform a real R2 delete after a head plus customMetadata.store_id ownership check (upload.ts:236-271).
findings.risk: A flat key space means any future code path that lists or serves by key without the database ownership check leaks cross-tenant PDFs containing customer names and addresses. 'Delete everything for store X' requires a full-bucket scan plus per-object metadata reads, which does not survive 10,000 merchants. A file declared image/png whose bytes are HTML or SVG is accepted and served from cdn.letbuyy.com. Absent lifecycle rules, objects orphaned by row deletion persist indefinitely — a cost and a DPDP retention exposure.
findings.recommendation: Prefix new object keys with site_id (the legacy-owner-key read path at upload.ts:97-99 already exists for back-compat), sniff magic bytes for the allowlist, define an R2 lifecycle policy, and add a per-site media index plus an orphan reconciliation job.
findings.trigger: Before the first DPDP erasure request, or before 1,000 merchants.
findings.verification: Falsify by exhibiting a site-prefixed key. Confirm by uploading a file with a false Content-Type and observing acceptance.

findings.title: Disaster recovery is declared policy only: no RTO, no RPO, no PITR, and the sole backup is a 7-day CI artifact produced only on deploy
findings.current_state: config/runtime/database-recovery-policy.json marks pointInTimeRecovery.status 'human-required-paid-tier' with skipId SKIP-W0-PITR-TIER; its resumeEvidence list requires an RPO/RTO target recorded and a restore timestamp tested in a non-production clone. Searching config/, infrastructure/, scripts/, database/ and docs/runbooks/, neither an RTO nor an RPO value is recorded anywhere. The only backup is production-deploy.yml:252-260 (pg_dump custom format, pg_restore --list, gpg AES256) uploaded at :262-269 with retention-days: 7, running only on a production deploy. scripts/governance/foundation-restore-drill.mjs:14-15 hard-refuses any non-localhost URL and :33 requires LETBUYY_RESTORE_DRILL_ALLOW_EXECUTE=true; no workflow calls it. pg_restore --list validates that the dump is readable, never that it restores. There is no database-restore runbook.
findings.expected_state: A commerce platform holding an immutable money ledger needs a stated RPO and RTO, PITR enabled, and at least one rehearsed restore.
findings.risk: If PostgreSQL is lost or corrupted between deploys, the recovery point is the last production deploy — potentially days of orders, payments and ledger entries — and the backup itself expires 7 days after that deploy. Recovery time is unknown because it has never been measured. A dump that lists cleanly can still fail to restore on extension, role, ownership or sequence failures. Restore time also grows with database size, which grows with the unpruned observability tables of ARCH-RESEARCH-012.
findings.recommendation: Founder decision to enable Supabase PITR (paid tier); record explicit RPO and RTO in database-recovery-policy.json; move the encrypted dump off the 7-day GitHub artifact into durable storage (R2 is already provisioned); add a scheduled job that restores the latest dump into the ephemeral PostgreSQL container and asserts table and sample row counts; write the missing restore runbook.
findings.verification: Confirm with a dated drill record showing measured RTO and asserted row counts.

findings.title: sessions.token stores the raw bearer credential in cleartext, including the full identity-issued ES256 JWT
findings.current_state: POST /auth/custom/sessions/create inserts the token directly: db.from('sessions').insert({ user_id, device_id, token, expires_at }) where token = providedToken || randomHex(32) and providedToken is the identity-issued ES256 JWT (routes/auth.ts:1141-1149). Validation then matches on the raw value: WHERE sessions.token = p_token (175:61). By contrast the rotation-events table correctly stores only SHA-256 hashes (old_token_hash, new_token_hash at 175:111-112) and customer password-reset tokens are hashed (customer-engagement-routes.ts:491), so the hashed pattern is understood elsewhere in the same codebase. A partial index idx_sessions_active_token on the raw token makes bulk extraction cheap.
findings.expected_state: A bearer credential should be stored as a hash so that read access to the table does not equal impersonation — exactly the pattern already used two tables over.
findings.risk: Any SELECT on public.sessions — a support query, a backup, a logical-replication stream, a read replica, or an over-broad service_role query in one of 114+ gateway files (ARCH-RESEARCH-001) — hands over live, directly usable merchant session bearers for up to 30 days. With rotation disabled (ARCH-RESEARCH-058) those tokens do not age out.
findings.recommendation: Store token_hash = encode(digest(token,'sha256'),'hex') and match on it in the RPC, migrate the index to the hash column, and never return the raw token from any read endpoint. The rotation-events table already models this exactly.
findings.verification: Falsify by finding a hash column in use. Confirm by SELECTing public.sessions.token and presenting the value as a bearer.

findings.title: All four Workers' default wrangler block shares the production Worker name, and the api-gateway default block is staging-flavoured with no bindings

findings.title: Merchant session rotation and token-reuse detection are implemented in the database but unreachable: both callers pass rotate:false, so a 30-day bearer never rotates
findings.current_state: validate_and_rotate_merchant_session gates both controls behind p_rotate (175_fix_session_rpc_search_path.sql:95-117 rotation, :37-56 reuse-detection, backed by session_token_rotation_events with UNIQUE old_token_hash at 161:21-33). The only two TypeScript callers pass { rotate: false }: services/api-gateway/src/middleware/auth.ts:136 and routes/auth.ts:387 — introduced that way by commit 8ceb83d1, the very commit that shipped the feature. session_token_rotation_events therefore stays empty, the reuse_detected revocation branch and the rotated_session_token cookie-refresh path (routes/auth.ts:410 -> identity-platform api/auth/session/route.ts:25-28) are dead, and MERCHANT_SESSION_ROTATION_INTERVAL_SECONDS = 600 (merchant-session.ts:39) is never consulted. Sessions are 30-day tokens (auth-core:127; identity-issued-session.ts:5; cookies.ts:85). Migration 175 is the final definition at this SHA; no later migration re-enables rotation.
findings.expected_state: Migration 161's own header states the intent: live merchant session idle timeout, rotation, reuse detection and revocation. Note this is a broken-own-design finding, not a constitutional violation — LETBUYY_CONSTITUTION.md nowhere mandates merchant session rotation.
assumptions: Only routes/auth.ts:387 is the actual defect. middleware/auth.ts:136 has no channel to return a new cookie to the browser, so rotate:false there is load-bearing and correct.

The remediation is materially larger than flipping a flag: three of the four consumers of GET /auth/custom/session discard rotated_session_token (identity-platform lib/auth/session.ts:45-73, mobile-bff index.ts:248, api-client index.ts:3888), so enabling rotation today would log those callers out every 10 minutes; and the RPC's rotation mints an opaque gen_random_bytes(32) token (175:98) that would displace the identity-issued ES256 token required in production (ARCH-RESEARCH-060).

Compensating controls are live: the 8h idle timeout does fire (175:84-93, :119-124); logout and logout-everywhere revocation work and are checked on every request (175:69-72); the cookie is httpOnly and is HMAC-re-wrapped in transit to the gateway (auth-core:621-646); refunds and payouts require step-up.
findings.risk: A stolen merchant session token is valid for up to 30 days with no rotation window that would surface theft, and token-reuse detection — the control that would catch a cloned cookie — never runs. This is a missing detection control behind live compensating controls, requiring prior token compromise.
findings.recommendation: Decide deliberately: either finish the design (rotation calls back into identity-platform for a freshly signed token, and all four session consumers propagate it) or delete the rotation branch, the rotation-events table and the interval constant so the codebase stops advertising a control it does not run.
findings.verification: Falsify by finding a caller passing rotate:true. Confirm by observing session_token_rotation_events row count remain zero in a live database.

findings.title: The six-digit OTP is brute-forceable: per-IP throttle only, no per-token or per-email attempt counter, and a non-atomic consume
findings.current_state: The OTP is 6 digits (randomOtp at routes/auth.ts:214-218, range 100000-999999). The only throttle is checkRateLimit('verify_otp', ip) — 5 attempts per 15 minutes keyed on x-forwarded-for (apps/identity-platform/src/app/api/auth/verify-otp/route.ts:20; lib/rate-limit.ts:43). The gateway's /custom/tokens/validate does a plain .eq('token', token).eq('type', type) lookup (auth.ts:1304-1311) with no attempt counter on the token row and no per-email throttle; the token is invalidated only on SUCCESS (update({used:true}) at :1333), never after N failures, and that update is a read-then-write rather than a conditional update.
findings.expected_state: A 6-digit email OTP that grants email-verified status and, via set-password, a full merchant session needs an attempt counter bound to the token or the identity, not to the caller's IP.
findings.risk: The keyspace is 10^6 and the throttle is per-source-IP. An attacker with 1,000 IPs gets 5,000 guesses per 15 minutes against a live OTP, and the token is never burned by failures. Success yields email-verified state and a password-set intent — account-creation control over the victim's address. The read-then-update also permits two concurrent successful consumes of one token.
findings.recommendation: Add an attempts column to verification_tokens, increment it on every validate call and hard-invalidate at 5. Key the identity-platform rate limit on the email as well as the IP. Make the consume atomic: UPDATE verification_tokens SET used=true WHERE id=$1 AND used=false RETURNING ... instead of SELECT-then-UPDATE.
findings.verification: Falsify by exhibiting a per-token attempt counter. Confirm with a distributed guessing test against staging.

findings.title: PostgreSQL mints session bearer tokens with gen_random_bytes on rotation — a second credential minter one boolean away from being switched on
findings.current_state: When p_rotate is true and the interval has elapsed, the RPC executes v_new_token := encode(gen_random_bytes(32),'hex') and writes it back as the live session token (175_fix_session_rpc_search_path.sql:98,:120). The credential replacing the identity-platform-issued ES256 JWT is therefore minted by the database with no issuer, audience, subject or signature. The branch is unreachable today because both callers pass rotate:false (ARCH-RESEARCH-058), but the code path is deployed. The gateway also mints randomHex(32) opaque session tokens directly when no identity token is supplied outside production (routes/auth.ts:1142, gated by isProductionGatewayRuntime at :1120-1127).
findings.expected_state: R-14 / IDN-R1: identity-platform is the sole token issuer; every other runtime — and the database — is verify-only.
findings.risk: Flipping rotate: true — a one-word change that looks like a security improvement and would pass every validator, since the sole-issuer validator scans only apps/services/packages and never .sql — silently demotes the merchant realm from identity-issued asymmetric tokens to database-issued opaque tokens after the first 10 minutes of every session. The ES256 signature would then be verified exactly once per login and never again.
findings.recommendation: If rotation is wanted, it must call back into identity-platform for a freshly signed token rather than generating one in SQL. Extend identity-sole-issuer-validator.mjs to scan database/supabase/migrations for token-minting patterns (gen_random_bytes written into a credential column), since it explicitly skips .sql files today.
findings.trigger: Before any change to the rotate flag.
findings.verification: Falsify by exhibiting a callback to identity-platform in the rotation branch. Confirm by reading 175:98.

A missing TURNSTILE_SECRET_KEY also returns false (security.ts:227-229; turnstile.ts:78-81). Fail-closed is the correct security posture; the absence of a deadline is the defect.

findings.title: The idempotency claim, the money RPC and the outbox emit are three separate transactions with no atomicity
findings.current_state: On every money route the sequence is: idempotency.begin INSERT (execution/idempotency-execution.adapter.ts:76), then the money RPC (a separate PostgREST call), then an outbox_events upsert (execution/event-execution.adapter.ts:60), then idempotency.complete UPDATE (:162). Each is its own transaction over Supabase REST. If the process dies after the RPC commits, the idempotency row stays 'processing' with a 120-second lock (:73), and on retry the caller receives ConflictError; after lock expiry it is re-claimed and the RPC re-runs — safe only because each RPC carries its own internal idempotency key.
findings.expected_state: Constitution: transactional OUTBOX. The event emit must commit in the same transaction as the state change it describes.
assumptions: The RPCs DO emit their own in-transaction outbox rows (170:550, 166:276), so the gateway-level emits are partly redundant duplicates on a different idempotency key — see ARCH-RESEARCH-026.
findings.risk: The gateway-level order.created and order.paid emits are not transactional with the state change; a crash between them loses the event with no replay source. The idempotency record can also record 'completed' for a request whose RPC actually failed, or stay 'processing' for a request that succeeded.
findings.recommendation: Drop the gateway-level outbox emits that duplicate an in-RPC emit, or move idempotency bookkeeping into the RPCs so claim, state change and outbox commit atomically. At minimum add a reconciliation sweep for idempotency_keys stuck in 'processing' whose resource actually exists. Removing two of the four write transactions per order-create and per payment-verify is also a 30-40% reduction in write round-trips on the two hottest money paths.
findings.verification: Falsify by exhibiting a single-transaction path. Confirm by killing the process between the RPC and the outbox write and observing the event is absent.

findings.title: The refund path is correctly gated and ledgered, but the gift-card restore is best-effort on a different route and outside the refund transaction
findings.current_state: complete_order_refund (168:311) locks the refund and order FOR UPDATE, rejects cumulative refunds exceeding the order total (168:365) and posts a balanced ledger transaction debiting merchant_payable and crediting refund_clearing (168:401). The merchant refund route requires step-up (routes/payments.ts:497), calls the provider before writing the ledger, and returns 502 with no ledger entry if the provider refund fails (:551-558). But gift-card restoration (restore_gift_card_on_refund, migration 174) is invoked only from the order status-transition route inside a try/catch that warns (routes/orders.ts:1200-1211) and from the COD cancel path (order-risk.ts:305-311) — never inside complete_order_refund, which migration 174:13 explicitly leaves untouched because it is validator-pinned. Partial refunds of gift-card orders are explicitly not handled (174:15-16).
findings.expected_state: Reversal of a gift-card-funded order should restore the redeemed balance in the same transaction that reverses the money.
findings.risk: A refund executed through complete_order_refund or POST /payments/:id/refund — rather than through the order status transition — never restores the gift-card balance, silently destroying customer value. Migration 174's own header documents this class of bug.
findings.recommendation: Call restore_gift_card_on_refund from inside complete_order_refund, proportionally for partial refunds, or make the refund route call it and fail the request when it errors rather than warning.
findings.trigger: Unconditional; first gift-card-funded refund through the merchant route.
findings.verification: Falsify by finding the call inside 168. Confirm with a behavioural test: refund a gift-card-funded order via /payments/:id/refund and assert the gift-card balance.

findings.title: Four compat ledgers retain live TypeScript writers while the canonical ledger is the declared single authority
findings.current_state: Four compatibility ledger surfaces retain live TypeScript writers despite ART-10 / R-15 designating the canonical double-entry ledger as the single authority. The money-ledger reconciliation job compares only wallet_ledger_entries against the merchant_payable balance (160:173, 198-256), so drift between the canonical ledger and the other compat surfaces is not measured at any latency.
findings.expected_state: ART-10 / R-15: one canonical ledger; compat ledgers retire once a reconciliation harness proves zero drift on the path they replace.
assumptions: Retirement is gated on the zero-drift proof of ARCH-RESEARCH-024, which cannot be produced from the repository.
findings.risk: Two money representations with only one comparison edge instrumented. Any divergence outside the wallet/merchant_payable pair is invisible.
findings.recommendation: Extend the reconciliation job's scope to every compat surface before retiring any of them, and hold retirement behind the ART-10 zero-drift proof.
findings.verification: Confirm by running a per-surface variance comparison against the canonical ledger.

findings.title: Two observability artifacts are dead config and eight runtime manifests assert an OpenTelemetry/Prometheus/Tempo/Loki/Grafana stack that no code implements
findings.current_state: infrastructure/observability/otel-collector.yaml has neither a producer nor a destination: it exports traces to tempo.letbuyy-observability.svc.cluster.local:4317 (:29) and logs to loki....:3100 (:33) — Kubernetes service DNS for a cluster that exists nowhere outside docs/archive — and no services/* or apps/* package.json carries any @opentelemetry dependency, no span is created and no /metrics route exists. infrastructure/observability/prometheus-rules.yaml:5,14,23 alerts on http_server_errors_total, http_requests_total, letbuyy_queue_dead_letter_total and letbuyy_deployment_health_gate_failed_total; all four have zero emitters repo-wide because the code emits dot-separated names (letbuyy.runtime.request at observability.ts:166, letbuyy.replay.lag.seconds at index.ts:604, letbuyy.queue.* at queue-workers/index.ts:318,342), and no Prometheus scrape target exists in infrastructure/cloudflare/*.tf or any workflow. Eight runtime.manifest.json files (api-gateway:111, queue-workers:94, webhook-service:91, mobile-bff:83, storefront-runtime:98, merchant-control-plane:95, marketing-site:94, platform-console:92) each state 'Emits correlated runtime telemetry to the OpenTelemetry, Prometheus, Tempo, Loki, and Grafana stack declared in infrastructure/observability'. verify-observability-rollout.mjs:32-57 asserts only string fragments and JSON structure and then prints 'observability verification passed'; that plan-mode branch is wired into staging-runtime-deployment.yml:70 and production-rollout.yml:133.
findings.expected_state: Either a live pipeline exists with emitters matching the alert expressions, or the platform config is honestly marked not-yet-provisioned rather than declaring mustUseLiveTelemetry.
assumptions: 'No live metric pipeline exists' is REFUTED. A real pipeline exists in source and config: RUNTIME_TELEMETRY Analytics Engine bindings are declared for staging AND production in all four Workers, the gateway writes an AE data point on the live request path (observability.ts:165-192) and inserts a runtime_telemetry_metrics row in the same handler, and queue-workers does the same. There is even an in-band alert enqueue at lib/runtime-alerting.ts:179-191.

The four Grafana dashboards are the ONE correctly-wired artifact: grafana-runtime-dashboard.json:19,31 query rawSql against runtime_telemetry_metrics for exactly the metric names the code emits, and line 19's dimensions->>'server_error_count' is genuinely written at observability.ts:284.
