The --execute path of verify-observability-rollout.mjs:63-65 does fail closed on missing PROMETHEUS_URL/GRAFANA_URL/OTEL_COLLECTOR_HEALTH_URL, and live-production-certification.json:5 self-labels 'credential-gated-plan-ready' — a partially honest marker.
config/runtime/observability-platform.json's mustUseLiveTelemetry:true field has NO consumer anywhere, so no gate turns green because of it.
findings.risk: Two dead artifacts plus false manifest assertions plus a file-existence gate create documented-but-nonexistent alerting. The three Prometheus alert rules would evaluate no-data forever even if Prometheus were deployed, because the metric names do not match. Every operational readiness claim built on 'observability' cites a stack that has never run.
findings.recommendation: Pick one: delete the Prometheus/Grafana/Loki/Tempo artifacts and build alerting on the Analytics Engine SQL API plus Workers Logs, which is what the topology actually supports; or provision the stack. Either way correct the eight runtime manifests, which assert a capability no runtime has, and add one deterministic assertion to the observability validator: every metric name referenced in prometheus-rules.yaml must appear as a metricName literal in a deployed runtime.
findings.verification: Falsify by finding an OTLP producer. Confirm by grepping the four alert metric names across services/ and apps/.

findings.title: Emitted telemetry has no reader and two of four Workers bind the telemetry dataset without writing to it, while Workers Logs head sampling discards roughly 90% of error logs
findings.current_state: Four emission sites write to the RUNTIME_TELEMETRY Analytics Engine dataset (observability.ts:165, index.ts:603, queue-workers/index.ts:317,341) and nothing reads it: the only reader-shaped code is packages/lcis-adapters/src/analytics-engine/AnalyticsEngineAdapter.ts, which at :48 declares verbatim that AE query values are NOT CONNECTED because the SQL API is POST-only and its GET-only boundary cannot reach it, and nothing outside that package references the adapter. No dashboard JSON queries Analytics Engine (all four use the postgres datasource uid supabase-ops); no script, workflow or route issues an AE SQL query. services/webhook-service binds RUNTIME_TELEMETRY in both environments (wrangler.toml:61-63,:100-102) and never calls writeRuntimeTelemetryDataPoint — its entire telemetry is 31 mostly-unstructured console.* lines; services/mobile-bff declares and binds it (src/index.ts:16; wrangler.toml:79-81,:127-129) with no write anywhere. Separately all four Workers set [observability] head_sampling_rate = 0.1 and [observability.logs] head_sampling_rate = 0.1 with invocation_logs = true in the default, staging and production blocks; head sampling selects invocations before the handler runs, so a 500 has the same 10% retention chance as a 200, and the console.error escalation for 5xx (observability.ts:85-86) cannot survive a sampling decision already made upstream.
findings.expected_state: Emitted telemetry should have at least one consumer — a dashboard, an alert evaluator or a scheduled query. The webhook worker handles the payment provider callback path and must emit signature-failure, replay-age and processing-latency metrics. Error and payment-path invocations should be retained at 100%.
findings.risk: The Analytics Engine path is the one telemetry channel that does not load PostgreSQL, and it is unused — so during an incident the fastest available answer source is a dataset nobody queries and responders fall back to 10%-sampled logs or to PostgreSQL tables that may themselves be the problem. The Razorpay webhook path, the single most security- and money-critical ingress, produces no metric at all, and 90% of its only telemetry is discarded. During an incident roughly nine out of ten error log lines simply do not exist.
findings.recommendation: Add a minimal Analytics Engine SQL query path (POST /accounts/{acct}/analytics_engine/sql with a scoped read token) behind the operations API and point the runtime dashboard at it — this is the lowest-cost route to a real, PostgreSQL-independent metric pipeline given the emitters already exist. Add the writeRuntimeTelemetryDataPoint plus structured-log pair to webhook-service for signature outcome, event age and per-event-type latency; either use or remove the mobile-bff binding. Raise head_sampling_rate to 1 for webhook-service and queue-workers (low volume, high diagnostic value).
findings.verification: Falsify by finding an AE reader or a webhook-service emission. Confirm by querying the dataset and by counting webhook-service metrics.

findings.title: validate:observability is a file-existence check, runbooks reference a metric that does not exist, and the highest-blast-radius procedures have no runbook
findings.current_state: package.json:53 maps validate:observability to scripts/validators/production-readiness-validator.mjs, whose assertions are exists()/shape checks: a requiredFiles array (:16-83) including otel-collector.yaml, prometheus-rules.yaml and the four Grafana JSONs asserted at :89, referenced-file existence at :185,:201,:207, and JSON key presence at :210-258. Separately the 17 files in docs/runbooks/ are mostly actionable and cite real routes and scripts that this author verified exist, but queue-dlq-redrive.md:9 instructs the operator to watch 'cloudflare.queue.delivery.lag' — a metric name that appears nowhere in the repository (the emitted names are letbuyy.queue.delivery.batch and letbuyy.queue.dead_letter.total), and deployment-rollback.md:9 conditions closure on error budget burn, which is computed nowhere (ARCH-RESEARCH-031). No runbook exists for restoring the database from the pg_dump artifact, for PostgreSQL connection exhaustion, for KV write-quota exhaustion, or for a Razorpay outage.
findings.expected_state: A validator named after observability should assert that emitted metric names match alert expressions and that every declared dashboard resolves to a datasource that exists. Runbooks should reference only signals that exist, and the highest-probability failure modes must each have one.
findings.risk: The file-existence check is the mechanism by which ARCH-RESEARCH-100's alert-name mismatch and unreachable collector both remained green, so a passing gate here is actively misleading evidence of operational readiness. An operator following the DLQ runbook during an incident will search for a metric that does not exist. The three missing runbooks map exactly to the three saturation ceilings identified in this register (KV write quota, PostgreSQL connections, provider outage), and the absence of a database-restore runbook leaves the one procedure with the highest blast radius entirely undocumented.
findings.recommendation: Add one deterministic assertion to the validator: every metric name referenced in prometheus-rules.yaml must appear as a metricName literal in the deployed runtimes, and every dashboard datasource uid must be declared in a tracked provisioning artifact. Correct the metric name in queue-dlq-redrive.md, remove or replace the error-budget condition in deployment-rollback.md, and write four runbooks: database restore from the encrypted dump, PostgreSQL connection exhaustion, KV write-quota exhaustion, and Razorpay outage.
findings.verification: Falsify by finding a name-matching assertion. Confirm by grepping the runbook metric names against the emitters.

findings.title: The automatic outbox relay is capped at 4,800 events/day, roughly 1.3-1.7x under the platform's own ratified 30k-orders/month target
findings.current_state: The production api-gateway cron is '*/15 * * * *' (wrangler.toml:236, 96 ticks/day, verified first-hand in evidence/02) and the scheduled handler calls outbox.dispatchBatch({ outboxLimit: 50 }) (index.ts:945-947, verified first-hand). claim_outbox_events hard-caps at LIMIT LEAST(GREATEST(p_limit,1),100) (000_baseline.sql:756) and is the ONLY definition across all 126 migrations. That is 50 x 96 = 4,800 events/day as an upper bound, with retries of failed rows consuming the same budget. Staging has crons = [] (:120). api-gateway declares only queue producers, never a consumer, and queue-workers' cron '17 */6' runs the inventory sweeper, ledger reconciliation, analytics rollup, incident reminders and compliance export — no outbox relay.
findings.expected_state: At the TOP of the constitutional envelope (~30,000 orders/month, LETBUYY_CONSTITUTION.md:110) an inferred ~6-8 outbox events per order lifecycle requires ~6,000-8,000 events/day of sustained relay capacity.
assumptions: This is a beta free-tier tuning value, not an architectural ceiling. The comment at wrangler.toml:235 records the pre-throttle value and commit ebaf61e2 changed */1 to */15 for cost. Restoring */1 yields 72,000 events/day and the RPC already permits 100/claim (144,000/day, or 9,600/day at the current cron without any cron change) — so the current setting uses half the available headroom.
It has no present impact: LETBUYY_CONSTITUTION.md:77 states zero production merchants, and at the 100- and 1,000-merchant tiers the ceiling has 6-60x headroom.

Two sub-claims are corrected. POST /operations/outbox/dispatch (routes/operations.ts:126-141) is a second, operator-triggered relay path, so the ceiling CAN be exercised in staging despite crons=[]. Order-confirmation emails do NOT traverse the outbox — they go direct to the bound NOTIFICATION_QUEUE (lib/order-confirmation-email.ts:127-130), so only merchant webhook deliveries and the platform_queue_jobs analytics/search fanout are gated by this ceiling.
The ~6-8 events/order figure is source-enumerated, not measured.
findings.risk: At the ratified target the relay ingests ~6,000-8,000 events/day against a 4,800/day ceiling, so outbox_events grows monotonically and event latency rises without bound past the 15-minute tick. The residual real gap is that no outbox-backlog age metric is emitted — the cron's only telemetry reads replay_operation_schedules (index.ts:557-563), not outbox age — so a backlog at scale accumulates unmonitored.
findings.recommendation: Raise the cron frequency and/or the per-tick limit toward the RPC's 100-row cap, loop dispatchBatch within a tick until claimed < limit, and emit an outbox-backlog age metric. Enable the staging cron so the relay is exercised pre-production.
findings.trigger: Sustained outbox arrival rate above 4,800/day, or oldest-unpublished outbox row age above 30 minutes.
findings.verification: Falsify by finding a second automatic relay. Confirm by measuring events/day dispatched against events/day created.

findings.title: Webhook delivery dispatch capacity is 4,800/day and processing is serial with no timeout — below one subscription per merchant at target order volume
findings.current_state: Outbound webhook deliveries are dispatched only from the api-gateway cron, which POSTs to webhook-service with limit: 50 (index.ts:961); webhook-service claims via claim_webhook_deliveries (RPC-capped at 100, 000_baseline.sql:968) and processes them SERIALLY in a for-loop with an awaited fetch per delivery (webhook-service/src/index.ts:651-680). At 96 ticks/day that is 4,800 deliveries/day. Fanout is one webhook_deliveries row per active matching subscription per event (execution/outbox-execution.adapter.ts:183-202), and every contracted domain event lists webhook-service as a consumer. max_attempts defaults to 10 (000_baseline.sql:1372) with a 120s exponential base.
findings.expected_state: At ~1,000 orders/day with even a single webhook subscription per merchant, sustained demand is ~8,000 deliveries/day.
assumptions: Demand is INFERRED from the event catalogue, not measured.
findings.risk: Demand exceeds capacity with one subscription per merchant, so webhook_deliveries accumulates permanent backlog. Serial processing makes it worse: 50 sequential HTTPS calls with no timeout (ARCH-RESEARCH-070) means one slow partner endpoint can consume the entire tick. With max_attempts 10 a partner outage multiplies claimed rows and crowds out healthy merchants — and with no tenant fairness (ARCH-RESEARCH-063) that crowding is unbounded.
findings.recommendation: Process claimed deliveries with bounded concurrency (Promise.all over chunks), add a per-request AbortSignal timeout, and raise the per-tick limit and/or cron frequency so sustained capacity exceeds expected deliveries/day. Add the per-tenant claim cap.
findings.verification: Falsify by finding a second dispatcher. Confirm by measuring deliveries/day dispatched against rows created.

findings.title: The email queue consumer is not idempotent per message and a mid-batch failure re-sends already-delivered transactional emails
findings.current_state: dispatchEmailDeliveries (services/queue-workers/src/index.ts:482-526) calls sendResendEmail (:503) with no lookup of an already-sent record and no Resend idempotency key (packages/infrastructure/resend-adapter/index.ts:52-75 passes no such header). It runs at :598 before the ack at :606, and the outer catch at :620-621 calls retry() on EVERY delivery in the batch. A Resend failure on message N of a multi-email batch — or the deterministic invalid-payload throw at :487, which is not quarantined — therefore re-sends the emails already delivered earlier in that batch, on each of up to 6 retries (queue-workers/wrangler.toml:294-300, max_batch_size 25). persistQueueBatch upserts distributed_queue_messages with status 'completed' at :575 BEFORE any email is sent, and that table is never read back.
findings.expected_state: A queue consumer must be idempotent per message: a redelivery of an already-processed message must not repeat an externally visible side effect. Cloudflare Queues guarantee at-least-once delivery, so this is a designed-for case.
assumptions: This is LATENT, not live: RESEND_API_KEY is never provisioned to queue-workers by the repository's own pipeline (production-deploy.yml:358-362 sets only INTERNAL_API_SECRET and QUEUE_TENANT_ENVELOPE_SECRET; the RESEND put at :329 targets api-gateway; grep -c RESEND services/queue-workers/wrangler.toml returns 0), so resendConfigured() is false and the loop logs missing-resend-secret and skips. An out-of-band `wrangler secret put` is UNKNOWN and unverifiable from here.

'Any throw anywhere later in the try block' is REFUTED: review-checks.ts:220-226, support-automation.ts:147-157, compliance.ts:195-207, executive-analytics.ts:459-473 and incident-command.ts:201-216 all catch per delivery, and risk-scoring.ts:242-246 skips non-risk job types before any I/O. The realistic trigger narrows to a Resend failure on message N>1 or the unquarantined invalid-payload throw.
The 19-duplicates figure requires 25 notification messages within the 10s max_batch_timeout, far above the governed envelope.
findings.risk: Once the secret is wired, one transient Resend 5xx mid-batch re-sends every email already delivered in that batch, on each retry — customer-trust damage plus spam complaints against a shared sending domain, degrading deliverability for all merchants. The adjacent and arguably higher-priority defect today is the inverse: because the producer binding IS present in production while the consumer has no key, production order-confirmation, cancelled and refunded emails appear to be silently dropped (ARCH-RESEARCH-085).
findings.recommendation: Fix the idempotency BEFORE the secret is wired, since enabling the path activates the defect: ack each message individually as it succeeds and retry() only the specific failed message, and record a per-idempotencyKey sent-marker checked before calling sendResendEmail.
findings.trigger: Before RESEND_API_KEY is provisioned to queue-workers.
findings.verification: Falsify by exhibiting a sent-marker check. Confirm with a fake MessageBatch test that fails message N and asserts messages 1..N-1 are not re-sent.

findings.title: Order-confirmation email is silently dropped when Resend is unconfigured while the queue job is marked processed and acked
findings.current_state: dispatchEmailDeliveries checks resendConfigured(env) — which treats any key containing 'placeholder' or 'skip_needs_human' as unset (services/queue-workers/src/index.ts:476-479) — and on failure writes an error log then continues past the delivery (:493-508). The batch then acks every message at :606, so the queue message is consumed and the job is recorded 'completed' in distributed_queue_messages even though no email was sent. The producer has the same shape: enqueueOrderConfirmationEmail warns and returns when neither NOTIFICATION_QUEUE nor a configured Resend key is present (lib/order-confirmation-email.ts:132-144). RESEND_API_KEY is provisioned to api-gateway but not to queue-workers.
findings.expected_state: A transactional customer email that cannot be delivered because of missing configuration should surface as a failed or pending job an operator can drain after fixing the secret, not be consumed as complete.
assumptions: Whether RESEND_API_KEY exists on the production queue-workers Worker by out-of-band provisioning is UNKNOWN. Under the deployment configuration this repository declares, it does not.
findings.risk: Every customer order-confirmation email is dropped and the message acked. The only signal is a console.error line; queue depth is zero, the dead-letter metric is zero, and distributed_queue_messages says completed. Discovery is by customer complaint, and because the message is acked it cannot be redriven once the secret is fixed.
findings.recommendation: Treat a missing provider secret as a retryable (non-deterministic) failure so the message stays in the queue and drains once provisioned, or route it to the DLQ so it is visible and replayable. Add a startup assertion that a production ENVIRONMENT with the notifications consumer bound has a non-placeholder Resend key.
findings.verification: Falsify by finding RESEND in queue-workers/wrangler.toml or its deploy step. Confirm by placing an order in a production-shaped environment and checking for the email.

findings.title: Post-commit event idempotency keys embed a per-request UUID, so retries create duplicate outbox events
findings.current_state: emitDomainEvent upserts on onConflict: 'idempotency_key' (execution/event-execution.adapter.ts:74) against a global UNIQUE constraint (000_baseline.sql:14619). But callers build keys that vary per HTTP request: emitOrderEvent uses ${eventType}:${siteId}:${orderId}:${input.requestId || crypto.randomUUID()} (routes/orders.ts:427) and emitStorefrontOrderCreatedEvent uses order.created:${storeId}:${orderId}:${requestId} (checkout-payment-routes.ts:195). The SQL path by contrast uses stable keys derived only from the aggregate — 'checkout.completed:' || v_order_id (000_baseline.sql:2196), 'order.created:' || v_order_id (166:299) — which dedupe correctly.
findings.expected_state: An outbox idempotency key must be a deterministic function of (event type, tenant, aggregate) so a client or gateway retry of the same logical operation conflicts and is deduped, exactly as the SQL path does.
findings.risk: A retried status transition or checkout confirm writes a second order.paid or order.created outbox row, which fans out to duplicate platform_queue_jobs and duplicate webhook_deliveries (deduped by (subscription_id, event_id), but event_id is freshly generated per row). Consequences: double-counted analytics rollups (increment_analytics_rollup is additive, not idempotent), duplicate merchant webhooks, and consumption of the constrained relay budget of ARCH-RESEARCH-081.
findings.recommendation: Drop requestId from these idempotency keys and derive them purely from eventType + siteId + aggregateId, matching the SQL emitters. Where a genuinely repeatable event needs distinguishing, use a stable business discriminator such as the status-transition target, never a random UUID.
findings.verification: Falsify by finding a stable key. Confirm by retrying one status transition and counting outbox rows.

findings.title: The stale inventory reservation sweeper is correctly wired but capped at 1,000 expirations per day on a 6-hourly cron
findings.current_state: The sweeper is genuinely wired as ART-15 requires: the queue-workers scheduled() handler calls runInventoryReservationSweeper under ctx.waitUntil (services/queue-workers/src/index.ts:632-646), which invokes expire_inventory_reservations with sweeperLimit (inventory-reservations.ts:26-29). The RPC releases inventory_levels.reserved and marks the reservation expired with reason 'ttl_expired' in one transaction using FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED (141:304-348). Configuration: INVENTORY_RESERVATION_SWEEPER_LIMIT='250' (wrangler.toml:255) on crons '17 */6 * * *' (:237) — four runs per day, hard-capped at 1,000 by the RPC's LEAST(...,1000).
findings.expected_state: ART-15 requires the sweeper WIRED — satisfied. Sustained capacity must also exceed the reservation expiry rate at the ~1,000 orders/day target, where abandoned checkouts typically outnumber completed orders.
assumptions: The abandoned-to-completed checkout ratio is INFERRED from general commerce experience, not measured here.
Because checkout collapses reserve and commit (ARCH-RESEARCH-014), the sweeper currently has almost nothing to sweep on the main path — its capacity matters only once that lifecycle is split.
findings.risk: 250 x 4 = 1,000 expirations/day. At ~1,000 orders/day with a 2-3x abandonment ratio, expiries plausibly reach 2,000-3,000/day and the sweeper falls permanently behind, leaving stock reserved against carts that will never convert — false out-of-stock and direct lost revenue. The 6-hour interval also means a reservation can sit expired-but-unreleased for up to 6 hours even when capacity is adequate. With no per-site cap (ARCH-RESEARCH-063) one tenant can starve the sweeper for others.
findings.recommendation: Raise the cron frequency to hourly or better and the limit toward the 1,000 RPC cap, loop until the RPC returns fewer rows than the limit, instrument actual expirations/day against the budget, and add the per-site cap.
findings.verification: Falsify by finding a higher limit. Confirm by measuring expired-but-unreleased reservation age.

findings.title: The runtime dead-letter queue is misclassified by a substring check, and WhatsApp is unreachable in production because queue-workers never sets the provider mode
findings.current_state: Dead-letter classification is a substring test: `const status = batch.queue.includes('dead-letters') ? 'dead-lettered' : 'completed'` (services/queue-workers/src/index.ts:365). The events/analytics/search/notifications DLQ is named letbuyy-dead-letters-production and matches; the runtime DLQ is named letbuyy-production-dead-letter-queue (wrangler.toml:316, consumer :318-324) and does NOT contain the substring, so its messages are classified 'completed', persisted with status 'completed' (:249-253), counted as zero in the letbuyy.queue.dead_letter.total metric (:283-296), and — because dispatchEmailDeliveries skips only status === 'dead-lettered' (:483) — remain eligible for email dispatch. A separate, correct singular check queueName.includes('dead-letter') exists in platform-queue-consumer.ts:365, so the two layers disagree. Separately services/queue-workers/wrangler.toml declares no WHATSAPP_PROVIDER_MODE, WHATSAPP_PROVIDER or TWILIO_* variables in any env block; the consumer constructs the adapter from this.env.WHATSAPP_PROVIDER_MODE (platform-queue-consumer.ts:730-740), normalizeMode falls back to isProductionRuntime ? 'live' : 'sandbox' (whatsapp-commerce-adapter/index.ts:146-147), twilioLiveConfigured is false with no credentials so available = false (:280), and the consumer records status 'failed' with WHATSAPP_UNAVAILABLE (:742-758) — while api-gateway production explicitly pins WHATSAPP_PROVIDER_MODE = 'sandbox' (wrangler.toml:277).
findings.expected_state: Dead-letter classification must be driven by the declared DLQ names in config/runtime/queue-lifecycle-manifest.json, which already lists deadLetterNames per environment, not by an ad-hoc substring of one of two naming conventions. Provider mode must be explicit per runtime and consistent across runtimes, and a sandbox send must not be recorded with a delivery-shaped status (R-22 / PAY-R10).
findings.risk: letbuyy.queue.dead_letter.total under-reports: everything that dead-letters from letbuyy-production-queue (max_retries 10) is silently recorded as a successful completion, so the runtime queue appears to have a zero dead-letter rate no matter how badly it fails — corrupting the primary signal an operator would use to detect retry amplification saturating the async tier. Separately every WhatsApp order-lifecycle and COD-confirmation notification produced by the queue worker is recorded 'failed' in production and never sent: the entire WhatsApp-first India channel is dark, discovered only by reading dispatch logs, and the mode divergence between the two runtimes means fixing one does not fix the other.
findings.recommendation: Replace the substring test with an explicit set of DLQ names sourced from config/runtime/queue-lifecycle-manifest.json and use the same source for both index.ts:365 and platform-queue-consumer.ts:365 so the two can never disagree again. Declare WHATSAPP_PROVIDER_MODE and WHATSAPP_PROVIDER explicitly in every queue-workers env block so the fallback is never exercised, add a validator that the value matches across api-gateway and queue-workers for the same environment, and change the sandbox return to a distinct status that cannot be counted as queued.
findings.verification: Falsify by finding a manifest-driven classification. Confirm by dead-lettering a runtime-queue message and reading its recorded status, and by attempting a WhatsApp send in a production-shaped queue-workers deploy.

findings.title: The step-up token is never consumed — one HMAC token authorizes unlimited refunds and payouts inside its 10-minute window
findings.current_state: Step-up is real cryptography, not a length check: a TOTP-verified challenge is persisted with the token hash and jti (routes/security.ts:186-215), and verifySensitiveActionStepUp recomputes HMAC-SHA256 over 'lb-stepup-v1.<payload>' and compares constant-time, binding action, actor, site and verified_at and enforcing a 10-minute window (lib/security-controls.ts:193-215). But verification performs NO database lookup: the step_up_challenges row and its jti are never marked consumed, and neither routes/payments.ts:497 nor routes/payouts.ts:576 records the jti against the refund. The token is also accepted from body.metadata.step_up_token (payments.ts:501), so it can land in request-body logs.
findings.expected_state: PAY-R7 / R-10: a step-up factor authorizes one sensitive action; the stored challenge should be single-use.
findings.risk: A compromised or leaked token authorizes every refund and payout release for that actor and site for ten minutes.
findings.recommendation: On successful verification, atomically transition the step_up_challenges row keyed by challenge_token_hash or jti from 'verified' to 'consumed' and reject when the transition does not apply. Remove the body.metadata.step_up_token fallback so the token travels only in a header. Cost is one indexed UPDATE per sensitive action.
findings.verification: Falsify by exhibiting a consume. Confirm by replaying one step-up token across two refunds.

findings.title: One AUTH_SECRET is deployed to six trust domains and is the signing key for the lb_accounts cookie that is guard 2 of 2 on the account-switch endpoint
findings.current_state: AUTH_SECRET is deployed to the api-gateway Worker (production-deploy.yml:315) and to all five Next apps (:443, matrix :400-409) including marketing-site, which has no identity role. That same value is the HS256 signing key for the lb_accounts cookie (apps/identity-platform/src/lib/auth/cookies.ts:13,176-180), and lb_accounts membership is guard 2 of 2 on POST /api/auth/switch (apps/identity-platform/src/app/api/auth/switch/route.ts:69-81), where guard 1 (:56-63) is only 'you hold some valid session'. Five `|| AUTH_SECRET` fallbacks remain in source (routes/checkout.ts:88, storefront/cart-routes.ts:307, routes/media.ts:60, routes/export.ts:174, webhook-service/src/index.ts:584) plus a direct use at routes/internal-console.ts:441. scripts/validators/session-security-validator.mjs is a hand-listed file allowlist (:28,42,53,57,65,75) covering none of these six sites, so the gate is green while SEC-R7 is violated verbatim.
findings.expected_state: AGENTS.md:233 (SEC-R7): no shared symmetric secret across trust domains; AUTH_SECRET MUST NOT be a fallback for any other secret; the webhook `|| AUTH_SECRET` fallback is named DEAD verbatim. apps/platform-console/src/lib/console-session.ts:24 correctly removed its fallback, proving the pattern is known and fixable.
assumptions: Four of the five named forgery consequences do NOT exist. WEBHOOK: production-deploy.yml:345 gives that Worker only INTERNAL_API_SECRET and no wrangler var supplies AUTH_SECRET, so index.ts:584 is unreachable dead code and webhook-service is not an AUTH_SECRET holder. EXPORT: INTERNAL_API_SECRET is deployed in both environments, so the third-position fallback is never selected. MEDIA: the fallback IS live-selected (MEDIA_UPLOAD_SIGNING_SECRET is in no deploy workflow) but the ticket it mints has no verifier — the /upload router authorizes by session plus site ownership. IMPERSONATION: `lb_imp_` appears only at its mint site, with no verifier anywhere.

CHECKOUT is partially refuted: production-deploy.yml:320 deploys CHECKOUT_SIGNING_SECRET so the fallback is not reached in production (assuming the GitHub secret is populated — unknowable from the repository); it IS reached in staging, where staging-deploy.yml sets AUTH_SECRET at :83 and no CHECKOUT_SIGNING_SECRET, making the handoff HMAC key and the lb_accounts key literally the same value. Even a forged handoff cannot tamper with amounts because checkout.ts:249-270 recomputes the cart digest from the database row.
Escalates to S1 if PRODUCTION_CHECKOUT_SIGNING_SECRET is unpopulated or if any of the six runtimes has a known environment-disclosure path; both are HUMAN-REQUIRED to determine.
findings.risk: Independent of any fallback: AUTH_SECRET disclosure from ANY of six runtimes — including marketing-site — restores the ART-06 account takeover. The chain is mechanically confirmed: an attacker self-registers (satisfying guard 1 in their own client), forges lb_accounts with AUTH_SECRET, POSTs /switch with any email_verified target, and route.ts:110-113 mints and sets that target's session. This is key-separation and blast-radius collapse, not a directly exploitable vulnerability.
findings.recommendation: Make CHECKOUT_SIGNING_SECRET, MEDIA_UPLOAD_SIGNING_SECRET and INTERNAL_API_SECRET hard-required and fail-closed, copying the getConsoleSessionSecret production pattern (console-session.ts:35-37), and delete all five `|| AUTH_SECRET` fallbacks. Give lb_accounts its own dedicated key so the /switch guard is not reachable from the platform-wide auth secret. Stop deploying AUTH_SECRET to marketing-site.
findings.verification: Falsify by showing AUTH_SECRET is not deployed to all six runtimes. Confirm by forging an lb_accounts cookie with a known AUTH_SECRET in staging and completing a /switch.

findings.title: Outbound webhook targets have no SSRF guard — validation is https plus a non-empty hostname and nothing else (SEC-R11)
findings.current_state: Target validation is literally `url.protocol === 'https:' && url.hostname.length > 0` (packages/notification-core/src/index.ts:505-512), applied identically at merchant registration (routes/notifications.ts:470,:512), fanout eligibility (execution/outbox-execution.adapter.ts:177) and dispatch (webhook-service/src/app-lifecycle-dispatch.ts:34-41, enforced :75). There is no DNS resolution, no allow/deny list, no private/loopback/link-local/ULA range check, no redirect policy (the default `follow` lets a merchant-controlled 302 escape the https-only rule) and no AbortSignal or timeout (:89-105). The path is live: the gateway cron (index.ts:952-961) calls webhook-service /webhook-deliveries/dispatch with limit 50, and the delivery loop (webhook-service/src/index.ts:648-658) is a sequential for-of with an await per delivery.
findings.expected_state: SEC-R11 (AGENTS.md:237) names the webhook SSRF explicitly (ISSUE-020) as a MUST-close-before-buyer-traffic item: a merchant-supplied outbound target must be validated against private, loopback, link-local and internal ranges before the request is issued, with a bounded timeout and a capped redirect policy.
assumptions: The exfiltration framing is REFUTED. The 2,000-character response preview IS persisted (webhook-service/src/index.ts:665,:674 -> webhook_deliveries.response_body_preview) but is NOT merchant-readable: no route selects that column; the only delivery-list route (routes/operations.ts:282-292) omits it and is gated by requireRoleCategory('ops') plus requireSuperAdmin; and RLS on webhook_deliveries is service_role/tenant-GUC only. This is BLIND SSRF from the merchant's position.

The cloud-metadata example is REFUTED for this topology: the dispatcher exists only as a Cloudflare Worker with no IMDS and no RFC1918-routable egress. That is a platform property of Workers, INFERRED rather than provable from this repository.
findings.risk: Blind SSRF probing of any Worker-reachable public or edge host from a merchant-controlled target, an https-only bypass via merchant-controlled redirect, unbounded per-request time on the money-event delivery path, and third-party response bodies landing in the tenant database. Because dispatch is sequential with no timeout, one deliberately slow target stalls the entire 50-delivery tick and can burn the cron invocation for every other merchant.
findings.recommendation: Extend isValidWebhookTarget to reject IP-literal hostnames in private/loopback/link-local/unique-local ranges and to reject localhost, *.local and *.internal; re-validate after DNS resolution at dispatch time to close the rebinding window; set redirect:'manual'; add an AbortSignal per delivery; and process deliveries with bounded concurrency instead of serially. Stop persisting third-party response bodies, or truncate to a status line.
findings.verification: Falsify by exhibiting range checks. Confirm by registering an internal-range https target in staging and observing the dispatch attempt.

findings.title: next.config declares Cache-Control: public, max-age=300 for ALL storefront paths while the Liquid path server-renders authenticated customer data
findings.current_state: apps/storefront-runtime/next.config.ts:122-129 applies Cache-Control: public, max-age=300, stale-while-revalidate=3600 to source '/:path*' with no exclusion for account, orders, cart or checkout, and no Vary: Cookie. In the Liquid render path renderLiquidPlan calls getStorefrontCustomerDrop(store.id, {includeOrders}) (src/lib/theme-engine/composition-engine.tsx:571), which resolves the HS256 customer session cookie server-side and injects name, email, addresses, orders and wishlist into the rendered HTML; /account, /account/orders and /account/addresses render exactly that.
findings.expected_state: Any response whose body varies with the customer session must be private, no-store, or at minimum non-shared-cacheable. A blanket public directive on /:path* is unsafe for a multi-tenant storefront with server-rendered account pages.
assumptions: Whether Next 16 or Vercel overrides this header for dynamically rendered App Router responses was NOT established at this SHA. send-payload.js:58-62 shows Next preserves a user-set Cache-Control, which makes the leak more plausible, not less — but the provider's edge behaviour is untestable without authorized access. This is the load-bearing unknown.
findings.risk: If any shared cache — Vercel edge, an intermediary proxy, or a merchant-fronted CDN on a custom domain — honours the declared header on a Liquid account page, one shopper's order history and address book can be served to another visitor of the same store for up to 5 minutes plus a 1-hour stale window. Even if Next currently overrides it, the configuration is one refactor away from the leak.
findings.recommendation: Scope the public, max-age=300 header to demonstrably anonymous paths and add explicit private, no-store for /store/:subdomain/account/:path*, /cart, /checkout and /orders. Verify the real Cache-Control on a live authenticated /account/orders response before closing this.
findings.trigger: Before Liquid account pages serve any real customer.
findings.verification: Confirm or falsify by requesting an authenticated /account/orders page against a deployed storefront and reading the response Cache-Control and Vary headers.

findings.title: The lb_accounts cookie is signed rather than encrypted despite carrying merchant PII for 90 days across every subdomain, CSRF is a JS-readable double-submit, and no audit record is written for any merchant authentication event
findings.current_state: encryptAccounts (apps/identity-platform/src/lib/auth/cookies.ts:173-180) builds new SignJWT({ accounts }).setProtectedHeader({ alg: 'HS256' }).sign(getSigningKey()) — a SIGNED JWT whose payload is base64url, not encrypted. The payload holds up to 10 entries of { email, name, avatar, lastLogin } (:71-76, :215), the TTL is 90 days (:28), and the cookie carries COOKIE_DOMAIN '.letbuyy.com' (production-deploy.yml:450) so it is sent to every platform subdomain. It is also guard 2 of 2 on /switch (ARCH-RESEARCH-069). setCsrfCookie sets letbuyy_csrf with httpOnly:false so the client can read it (:139-147), and validateCsrf accepts either letbuyy_csrf or the legacy lb_csrf cookie, comparing with plain === on values of length >= 16 (csrf.ts:11-24); the token is not bound to the session. Separately, a case-insensitive search for 'audit' across apps/identity-platform/src returns nothing, and services/api-gateway/src/routes/auth.ts contains no write to audit_logs for /custom/sessions/create, /sessions/destroy, /sessions/destroy-all or /users/authenticate — the only auth telemetry is a fire-and-forget new-device email and console.error. By contrast platform-console DOES audit its login/MFA/logout (console-auth-server.ts:208-238) and the customer realm writes activity rows (customer-engagement-routes.ts:76).
findings.expected_state: A cookie named and commented as encrypted should be encrypted (JWE) if it carries PII, and an authorization credential should not double as a PII carrier with a 90-day lifetime across every subdomain. The realm that suffered a documented account-takeover should record who switched into which account, from which IP and device, and when.
assumptions: decryptAccounts currently fails CLOSED, returning [] on verification failure so [].some(...) yields 403 — the naming is misleading but the behaviour is safe today.
SameSite=strict on the CSRF cookie carries most of the real protection.
findings.risk: Anyone who obtains the lb_accounts cookie — a subdomain XSS, a proxy log, a shared-device browser profile — reads a merchant's full multi-account email list in cleartext (DPDP-relevant personal data) for up to 90 days, and the misleading encrypt/decrypt naming means a future reviewer will assume confidentiality that does not exist. Any XSS on an accounts-domain page also reads the CSRF token directly, and because the token is not session-bound a token minted for one session is accepted for another. If AUTH_SECRET leaks or the /switch guard regresses there is no durable record from which to determine which accounts were entered, by whom, or when — the exact forensic question an account-takeover incident asks.
findings.recommendation: Switch lb_accounts to JWE with a dedicated key, or reduce the payload to opaque account identifiers resolved server-side; rename encryptAccounts/decryptAccounts to signAccounts/verifyAccounts; separate the /switch proof from the PII carrier. Bind the CSRF token to the session (HMAC of the session id under a dedicated key) and drop the lb_csrf fallback. Emit an audit row on session create, switch, logout and logout-everywhere carrying actor, target, IP, device fingerprint and outcome, reusing the console's existing audit-logs shape.
findings.verification: Falsify by finding JWE encryption or an auth audit write. Confirm by base64url-decoding an lb_accounts cookie payload.

findings.title: The JTI replay cache for cross-service signed requests is a per-isolate in-memory Map, and the merchant JWT's own jti is never recorded
findings.current_state: Internal-auth replay protection is `const consumedInternalJtis = new Map<string, number>()` at module scope in the Worker (services/api-gateway/src/lib/internal-auth.ts:79), swept lazily with a 5-minute maxAge (:90-98). It backs verifyInternalSessionHeaders (:123), verifyInternalAppRequest (:162) and verifyInternalIdentityPayload (:191). No KV, D1 or PostgreSQL is involved. Separately the merchant ES256 token carries a jti (apps/identity-platform/src/lib/auth/identity-issued-session.ts:67) but the gateway verifier only checks typeof jti === 'string' && jti.length >= 16 (lib/identity-session-verifier.ts:74-76, :101-103) — the value is never persisted or compared. The same per-isolate pattern is used for the queue circuit breaker (platform-queue-consumer.ts:233) and the KV query-cost backoff (rateLimit.ts:613).
findings.expected_state: A replay cache for cross-service signed requests must be shared across all serving instances. Cloudflare Workers run many independent isolates per colo and across colos; module-scope state is per-isolate and evicted at will.
findings.risk: A captured internal-auth request (signature plus JTI plus timestamp) can be replayed against a different isolate within the 5-minute freshness window and will be accepted, because the second isolate's Map is empty. The affected surface includes /auth/custom/sessions/create and /auth/custom/users/*, i.e. session minting. The merchant JWT's jti provides no replay protection at all — it is a presence check that satisfies a validator, not a control. The same isolate-scoped weakness makes the queue circuit breaker's protection proportional to isolate lifetime rather than to the failure.
findings.recommendation: Move the JTI cache to the CACHE KV namespace (already bound) or to a PostgreSQL table with UNIQUE(jti) and a TTL sweep, keyed by kind:jti; or shorten the freshness window materially. State explicitly in code that the merchant jti is not a replay control. Back the queue circuit breaker with shared state if the downstream it protects matters.
findings.verification: Falsify by finding durable JTI storage. Confirm by replaying one internal-auth request until it lands on a fresh isolate.

findings.title: Inbound provider webhooks enforce no timestamp or replay window, and replay_window_seconds is declared in the schema but never read
findings.current_state: The Razorpay handler verifies HMAC-SHA256 with timingSafeEqual before anything else (services/webhook-service/src/index.ts:718-736), then explicitly declines to enforce an age limit: a comment at :752-753 states idempotency is enforced by payment_webhook_events so age is not rejected, and an event older than 300s produces only a console.warn (:754-758). webhook_subscriptions.replay_window_seconds exists with a 60-86400 CHECK constraint (148_executable_notifications_router.sql:56, 84-85) but a repo-wide grep finds it only in SELECT column lists (routes/notifications.ts:450, 487, 524) — never compared against anything. The outbound signer emits X-LetBuyy-Timestamp and signs timestamp.body (app-lifecycle-dispatch.ts:53-55, 85-86), but verifyLetBuyyWebhookHmac (:57-63) checks only the signature.
findings.expected_state: SEC-R5 requires signature verification plus a timestamp/replay window plus idempotency recording before mutation. The ordering requirement IS met — writeWebhookEvent upserts payment_webhook_events and short-circuits on duplicate before any order or ledger mutation (index.ts:766, :774).
assumptions: Idempotency substantially mitigates replay: a re-sent captured event is deduped by (provider, provider_event_id). The residual is that when razorpayProviderEventId finds no payment/refund/order id the fallback key is event:created_at:signature[0..24] (:111-116), so an old signed body could be replayed indefinitely if the dedupe row is ever pruned by retention.
findings.risk: The dedupe table is currently the only replay defence, which makes its retention window a capacity/cost tradeoff with a direct security consequence. A declared-but-unenforced replay_window_seconds column is worse than none, because a reader assumes it is enforced.
findings.recommendation: Either enforce replay_window_seconds in verifyLetBuyyWebhookHmac and in the provider ingress handlers, or drop the column so no one relies on it. Confirm the retention policy for payment_webhook_events never prunes rows inside the window a provider may still retry.
findings.trigger: Before any retention policy is applied to payment_webhook_events.
findings.verification: Falsify by finding a comparison against replay_window_seconds. Confirm by replaying an old signed webhook body whose dedupe row has been removed.

findings.title: Non-production identity and checkout signing fall back to hardcoded literals, so staging cannot prove the production security posture
findings.current_state: checkoutSigningSecret (duplicated verbatim at routes/checkout.ts:87-92 and storefront/cart-routes.ts:306-311) resolves CHECKOUT_SIGNING_SECRET, then AUTH_SECRET, then STORE_ACCESS_SIGNING_KEY; if that value is missing or starts with SKIP_NEEDS_HUMAN_, it returns null ONLY when ENVIRONMENT or APP_ENV equals 'production' — otherwise it returns the literal 'letbuyy-local-sandbox-checkout-handoff-secret'. The gateway sets ENVIRONMENT='staging' for staging (wrangler.toml:123) and config/env/staging.env.example:26 ships CHECKOUT_SIGNING_SECRET as a SKIP_NEEDS_HUMAN placeholder. Separately isProductionIdentityRuntime returns true only when the env literal is exactly 'production' (apps/identity-platform/src/lib/dev-auth-bypass.ts:13-18), so on staging or a Vercel preview: getSigningKey falls back to the hard-coded literal 'dev-only-insecure-auth-secret-set-AUTH_SECRET-in-prod' when AUTH_SECRET is short or unset (cookies.ts:19-23); createIdentityIssuedMerchantSessionToken returns null instead of throwing (identity-issued-session.ts:41-46); and cookies are set with secure:false (cookies.ts:63). The gateway independently permits token-less session creation outside production (routes/auth.ts:1120-1127), so a staging login mints an opaque randomHex(32) session with no signature. A third definition problem compounds this: rateLimit.ts:58-67 and featureFlags.ts:13-17 define isProductionRuntime differently, and every wrangler env block sets NODE_ENV='production' including staging, so on the staging Worker the feature-flag helper reports production while the rate-limit helper reports non-production and uses an in-memory limiter.
findings.expected_state: Handoff and identity signing keys must be per-environment, purpose-scoped, and absent-means-fail-closed in every non-local environment. One shared runtime-environment predicate should be used by every gate so staging exercises the same code paths as production.
assumptions: In production the checkout fallback is not reached because CHECKOUT_SIGNING_SECRET is deployed at production-deploy.yml:320 — assuming the GitHub secret is populated, which is unknowable from the repository.
findings.risk: On staging, anyone can forge a checkout handoff and an lb_accounts cookie from secrets published in this repository, cookies travel without Secure, and the asymmetric issuance path — the single most important identity invariant — is never exercised before production. The staging E2E suite that gates every production release also runs against an in-memory rate limiter, so it cannot reproduce the 503 class of failure that took production /v1 down on 2026-08-01. Staging green is systematically not evidence for production, and the repository's own runbook says so.
findings.recommendation: Remove the hardcoded literals and the AUTH_SECRET/STORE_ACCESS_SIGNING_KEY fallbacks; fail closed in every environment except a locally detected dev runtime; de-duplicate checkoutSigningSecret into one module. Add 'staging' and 'preview' to isProductionIdentityRuntime or invert it to fail-closed unless an explicit dev flag is set. Extract a single exported runtimeEnvironment() helper used by both middlewares, and set RATE_LIMIT_KV_FALLBACK in [env.staging.vars] so staging traverses the real backend selection.
findings.trigger: Unconditional; precondition for trusting the staging E2E gate.
findings.verification: Falsify by exhibiting fail-closed behaviour on staging. Confirm by signing a staging checkout handoff with the published literal.

findings.title: checkout.letbuyy.com is declared as the hosted checkout origin, has no serving implementation, and 'checkout' is absent from every enforced reserved-name list — a merchant can permanently claim it
findings.current_state: This author re-verified that `rg checkout packages/tenant-core/src/index.ts` returns ZERO hits: 'checkout' is absent from RESERVED_STOREFRONT_LABELS (:27-44, 16 labels) and RESERVED_SUBDOMAINS (:46-57). resolveStorefrontHost (:134-136) therefore returns {kind:'subdomain', subdomain:'checkout'} for that host; SubdomainSchema's refine (:155-163) accepts it; POST /stores validates with CreateStoreSchema (routes/stores.ts:647, mounted index.ts:793) with no other name gate; and sites carries only a UNIQUE index on subdomain (000_baseline.sql:15756-15760) with no reserved-name CHECK or trigger in any later migration. store-context.ts:206-216 would map the host to the squatter's site and proxy.ts:321-322/:404 would serve it. The gateway mints handoffs to that exact host (wrangler.toml:286 CHECKOUT_ORIGIN; cart-routes.ts:567 new URL('/checkout', checkoutOrigin(c))), and apps/storefront-runtime has no top-level /checkout route — only /store/[subdomain]/checkout — so every signed checkout URL resolves to a 404 today. The 16-label list is deepEqual-pinned by tests/contracts/reserved-subdomain.test.ts:19-46 and re-asserted by reserved-subdomain-single-source-validator.mjs:16-31, so the omission is gate-locked, not accidental drift.
findings.expected_state: ART-14 requires a real hosted checkout.letbuyy.com origin with cart-bound signed handoff. A platform-owned origin must be in the reserved label set so no tenant can claim it, and must be bound to a named deploy target.
assumptions: 'Provisioned' is not established: infrastructure/dns/dns.tf:91-98 DECLARES the CNAME in Terraform. Live apply and the Vercel host attach are open human items (SKIP-D5-DNS-TERRAFORM-APPLY, SKIP-D6, HR-DNS-CHECKOUT), and tests/executable/human-required-live-paths.test.mjs:9 is test.skip. Configuration is not deployment.

No buyer is routed to that host today: no root /checkout route exists, no Vercel project binds it, and handoff minting 503s without CHECKOUT_SIGNING_SECRET (cart-routes.ts:540-544). The payment-hijack consequence is contingent on the DNS and host-attach step the repository records as not performed. This escalates to S1 the moment the host is attached.

The SQL reserved_words array (000_baseline.sql:8074-8084) also omits 'checkout' and additionally diverges from tenant-core by eight labels (apps, themes, developer, dcv, connect, status, docs, dev) — but validate_subdomain has ZERO callers, so it is list divergence, not a bypassed live guard. Two of those eight are provisioned platform infrastructure: connect has a DNS CNAME at dns.tf:132 and dcv is the domain-control-validation label.
findings.risk: A merchant who registers the subdomain 'checkout' takes durable, self-serve, irreversible ownership of the hostname the Constitution designates as the platform's payment origin, permanently blocking the constitutionally required cutover. At the moment DNS and host attach land it becomes a phishing-grade takeover of the exact origin buyers are taught to trust. Separately, if any future refactor routes store creation through the SQL validator, merchants become able to claim dcv.letbuyy.com and connect.letbuyy.com, which would break custom-domain control validation platform-wide.
findings.recommendation: Add 'checkout' (and 'pay', 'secure') to RESERVED_STOREFRONT_LABELS immediately, update the deepEqual-pinned contract test and the single-source validator in the same change, and audit existing sites for the label. Delete public.validate_subdomain (it has no callers) or regenerate its array from tenant-core, and extend reserved-subdomain-single-source-validator.mjs to assert that every hostname label provisioned in infrastructure/dns/dns.tf is reserved and that any SQL reserved-word array set-equals RESERVED_SUBDOMAINS.
findings.trigger: Before the DNS apply and Vercel host attach; ideally immediately, since the squat is pre-emptible today.
findings.verification: Falsify by finding 'checkout' in any enforced list. Confirm by attempting POST /stores with subdomain='checkout' against staging.

findings.title: No tenant fairness exists in any work-claiming path — one hot merchant delays every other
findings.current_state: All four live work-claiming functions order strictly by arrival time across the whole multi-tenant table with no site_id term and no per-site cap: claim_outbox_events (000_baseline.sql:754), claim_platform_queue_jobs (:822), claim_webhook_deliveries (:966), expire_inventory_reservations (141:323). No later migration changes this — the only other claim function added after the baseline is claim_payout_statement_release (160:357) — and the partition migrations partition by RANGE(created_at), not by tenant (081:36). All four are on live paths under the api-gateway cron '*/15 * * * *' and the queue-workers cron '17 */6 * * *'. The consumer adds no tenant dimension (platform-queue-consumer.ts:400-430). findings.title: Selected S3 residuals: cache stampede, ledger writer attribution, cart-binding subtotal, global idempotency uniqueness, missing FORCE on four rollup tables, and dead-configuration flags
findings.current_state: Six independently small residuals, grouped so they are tracked without inflating the register. (1) cachedJson has no request coalescing and no serve-stale path — on a Cache API miss it calls producer() unconditionally (storefront-cache.ts:121-129) and stale-while-revalidate is only a header string (:13, :24-26); with a 60s TTL, a KV-propagated (therefore staggered, not synchronised) version bump, the Next data layer above it and a 5-connection pooled cap below it, this is a scale-hardening efficiency gap, not a stampede. (2) Four gateway TypeScript call sites author arbitrary canonical ledger line-sets (lib/payment-route-support.ts:185, routes/payouts.ts:195, routes/commission.ts:148, routes/settlements.ts:175) and writer_module is never explicitly set, so the CHECK at 139:113 pins only the column default and provides no attribution. (3) canonicalCheckoutCartBinding (packages/checkout-core/src/index.ts:510) includes per-line unit_price_minor and line_total_minor and sorted coupon codes but no aggregate subtotal term, and the signed URL is a reusable bearer capability for its 10-minute life with no nonce. (4) outbox_events carries UNIQUE(idempotency_key) and platform_queue_jobs UNIQUE(queue_name, idempotency_key) with no site_id (000_baseline.sql:14619, :14739), unlike refund_transactions which correctly uses ON CONFLICT (site_id, idempotency_key) (:3207). (5) 169_internal_os_executive_analytics_rollups.sql:153-156 enables RLS on metric_rollups, mrr_arr_rollups, cohort_snapshots and funnel_steps without FORCE. (6) FEATURE_LIQUID is configured in all three wrangler environments and read by no runtime code — no featureGate is ever constructed for it and the real switch is the compile-time constant THEME_LIQUID_RENDERING_DEFAULT_ENABLED (packages/theme-engine/src/theme-governance.ts:14); storefront cache-version KV keys are written with no TTL and a read failure silently degrades to version '0' (storefront-cache.ts:75, :89), which serves the oldest cached generation rather than bypassing the cache; and razorpayx survives only as residual CHECK-constraint enum values on three frozen app-platform tables (000_baseline.sql:8293, :8295, :10263) tracked under SKIP-RAZORPAYX-ENUM-PURGE.
findings.expected_state: Each item has a named rule or an obvious correct form: single-flight is engineering judgment (no governance document mandates it); R-6 requires the ledger writer identity recorded; ART-14 specifies the HMAC binds sorted line items plus coupons plus subtotal; tenant-scoped uniqueness should include site_id; Constitution requires ENABLE+FORCE; and configuration that has no effect should be deleted.
assumptions: The global idempotency uniqueness is not currently exploitable because every key embeds a server-generated UUID; the risk is latent for any future emitter deriving a key from merchant-controlled input.
The razorpayx enum values cannot be written because no route reaches those tables behind the fail-closed app-platform kill switch; the residual is a re-enablement hazard.
The four 169 rollup tables carry no tenant column and hold platform-global metrics.
findings.risk: Individually minor. Collectively they are the class of residual that becomes load-bearing at the 1,000-to-10,000-merchant step or the moment a frozen surface is un-frozen: no origin-load damping at TTL expiry, no forensic attribution on the money ledger, a replayable checkout URL, a shared cross-tenant key space, tables that can be read by their owner role, and configuration that misleads an operator into believing a switch exists.
findings.recommendation: Add an in-isolate single-flight map around cachedJson; move the four TypeScript ledger postings behind purpose-specific SECURITY DEFINER RPCs and make post_ledger_transaction take an explicit writer_module; add an explicit subtotal_minor term to the cart binding and bind the handoff to a cart_token cookie or one-time nonce; migrate both idempotency constraints to include site_id and add a validator requiring site_id in any ON CONFLICT on a tenant table; add FORCE to the four 169 tables; delete FEATURE_LIQUID from the three var blocks and the flag union; make a KV read failure bypass the cache with a unique sentinel rather than falling back to '0'; and ship the razorpayx enum purge.
findings.trigger: Individually unconditional but low priority; revisit before the 1,000-merchant step.
